explanations.explanation: That's the ones, friend. Jesus says the Son of Man will be delivered over to the chief priests and scribes (Matthew 20:18). He says it plain, with no sprinkles on top to make it prettier. I think the Twelve got quiet real fast after that.

I see why you'd go there, since Jesus did sit and eat with tax collectors and sinners (Matthew 9:10). But that's a different scene from this one. Here He says the Son of Man will be delivered over to the chief priests and scribes. Tax collectors don't come up in His words at all.

explanations.answer: The merchants of Tyre and Sidon
explanations.explanation: Tyre and Sidon never show up in this talk, friend. Jesus doesn't mention a single merchant on that road. He says the Son of Man will be delivered over to the chief priests and scribes. That's a long way from the market, and honestly it's a heavy thing to say out loud.

True, and Jesus says it Himself. He tells the Twelve, "They will condemn Him to death" (Matthew 20:18). He's not hinting or dropping a riddle here. He lays it out ahead of time, which tells me He knows exactly where this road goes.

This one is actually true, friend. Jesus says the chief priests and scribes "will condemn Him to death" (Matthew 20:18). Those are His own words, right there in the verse. It's hard to read, and I don't blame anybody for hoping it said something else.

Gentiles it is, the non-Jewish nations. Jesus says they will "deliver Him over to the Gentiles" (Matthew 20:19). So He's handed over first to the chief priests and scribes, and then on to the Gentiles. Jesus lays out the whole order before it happens.

Samaritans make a fair guess, but they aren't in this verse. Jesus says the chief priests and scribes will deliver Him over to the Gentiles (Matthew 20:19). That's the word to hold onto here. I once stamped a whole batch with the wrong cutter, so I know how a close guess feels.
Levites aren't in this verse, friend. Jesus says they will deliver Him over to the Gentiles (Matthew 20:19). He doesn't mention a Levite anywhere in this talk. The word you want is Gentiles.

explanations.answer: He will be raised to life
explanations.explanation: Yes, and this is the best part of the whole announcement. Jesus says, "On the third day He will be raised to life" (Matthew 20:19). He mentions the hard things, and then He tells them it doesn't end there. Always read to the end of the sentence, baker.

explanations.answer: He will go back to Galilee
explanations.explanation: Galilee isn't what Jesus says here. His words are, "on the third day He will be raised to life" (Matthew 20:19). The third day is about being raised, not about a trip back home. I'd say that's a pretty big difference from a travel plan.

explanations.answer: He will hide in the wilderness
explanations.explanation: No hiding in what Jesus says. He tells the Twelve, "on the third day He will be raised to life" (Matthew 20:19). That's Him telling them exactly how it turns out, and there's no wilderness in the plan. I think those words were meant to hold the disciples up.

explanations.answer: One sits at His right and one at His left
explanations.explanation: That's the ask. She says, "Declare that in Your kingdom one of these two sons of mine may sit at Your right hand, and the other at Your left" (Matthew 20:21). Those are the two seats right beside Jesus, and she wants her sons in both of them. She walked in with a very specific request, I'll give her that.

explanations.answer: Both of them lead the other ten disciples
explanations.explanation: She doesn't say anything about leading the other ten. Her request is that one son sit at His right hand and the other at His left (Matthew 20:21). It's about seats next to Jesus, not about running the group. Still, I bet the other ten had opinions about it, and we'll get there.

explanations.answer: Both of them stand guard at His palace gate
explanations.explanation: No gate and no guard duty in her request. She asks that one son sit at His right hand and the other at His left in His kingdom (Matthew 20:21). Nobody in this passage mentions a palace. Standing guard is a job, and she was asking for a seat.

"We can," the brothers answer, quick as that (Matthew 20:22). No pause and no "let us think about it." I think they had no idea how big that cup was. Jesus follows up and says they will indeed drink His cup (Matthew 20:23).

"We will try" is a humble answer, but it's not what they say. The brothers answer, "We can" (Matthew 20:22). They say it straight and sure, with no wiggle room. I've said "I can!" at the oven door before I knew what was inside, so I get it.

They don't ask for more time, friend. The brothers answer, "We can" (Matthew 20:22). It comes out fast and confident. Whether they understood the whole cup, I can't say, but they sure answered like they did.
It's the other way around, friend. Jesus tells them, "You will indeed drink My cup" (Matthew 20:23). So the cup does come to the brothers. What He holds back is the seats, which aren't His to grant.
False, and you read it right. Jesus says, "You will indeed drink My cup" (Matthew 20:23). So the brothers' "We can" gets a yes. Only the seats are left open, because those aren't His to grant.

Father, right on the money. Jesus says, "These seats belong to those for whom My Father has prepared them" (Matthew 20:23). The seats are the Father's to give, and Jesus says so plainly. I love how He doesn't hand out a seat just because somebody's mama asked nicely.

Not disciples, friend. Jesus says the seats belong to those for whom "My Father has prepared them" (Matthew 20:23). The Father does the preparing, not the disciples. If it were up to the Twelve, I'm pretty sure there'd have been a lot more arguing.
Prophets aren't in this verse. Jesus says the seats are for those for whom "My Father has prepared them" (Matthew 20:23). The Father is the one doing the preparing. The word you want is Father.

Indignant is the word. The ten "were indignant with the two brothers" (Matthew 20:24). That means they were stirred up and not happy about what the brothers had asked. Picture the whole group going quiet and then all talking at once.

Pleased is not how the ten took it. The text says they "were indignant with the two brothers" (Matthew 20:24). They weren't clapping for anybody. I think nobody likes it when someone else grabs the best spot in line.
Patient would have been nice, but that's not what the text says. The ten "were indignant with the two brothers" (Matthew 20:24). Indignant means they were upset about it. I bet that was a loud walk.

True. Jesus says, "You know that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them" (Matthew 20:25). He's pointing at how rulers act so He can show a different way. And that different way is coming in the very next verse.

This one is true, friend. Jesus says, "You know that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them" (Matthew 20:25). He holds that up as the example of how not to do it. Then He says, "It shall not be this way among you" (Matthew 20:26).

Servant, and what a flip that is. Jesus says, "whoever wants to become great among you must be your servant" (Matthew 20:26). Greatness shows up as serving. It's the opposite of lording it over people.

Leader sounds right, and the brothers' mama might have picked it too. But Jesus says, "whoever wants to become great among you must be your servant" (Matthew 20:26). He turns greatness upside down. The word is servant.

Teacher is a nice word, but it's not the one here. Jesus says, "whoever wants to become great among you must be your servant" (Matthew 20:26). Greatness comes through serving. I'm a stamper, and I've learned that holding the dough steady beats being the fanciest cutter on the counter.

explanations.answer: Serve and give His life as a ransom for many
explanations.explanation: That's it, and it's the heart of the whole passage. Jesus says the Son of Man came "to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many" (Matthew 20:28). He's not asking them to do anything He isn't doing first. The greatest one in the room is the one who serves.

explanations.answer: Rule and raise up an army to free the many
explanations.explanation: An army is not the plan Jesus describes. He says the Son of Man came "not to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many" (Matthew 20:28). No army and no throne in that sentence. I think that's why it stops people in their tracks.

explanations.answer: Judge and cast down the rulers of the Gentiles
explanations.explanation: Jesus brings up the rulers of the Gentiles, but only to show how things shouldn't work among His own. Then He says the Son of Man came "to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many" (Matthew 20:28). He doesn't say anything about casting rulers down here. He says He came to serve.
